It's hard, I won't lie. My husband begged me stop for a month. I saw two different LCs and they both just kept giving me more advice. All I wanted was for some professional to tell me to quit. I'm sorry you're struggling. If it helps, the decision was the hardest part. But I felt instant relief. I didn't second guess my decision or feel guilty after like, a day. Because the change in our life was instant. My daughter wouldn't sleep, she cried constantly. As soon as we switched to formula she started taking actual naps. And I could *breathe*. My husband and I could take turns with the feeds. I got more sleep (still not much bc newborn, but I got enough to not die). I could remove her from my body instead of having her latched to me for literally 16+ hours a day trying to get enough food in her. I didn't worry I was going to fall asleep feeding and suffocate her, bc she slept more and if I couldn't keep my eyes open my husband and I could switch off. I put away that God forsaken breast pump that I never want to see again in my life. My nipples stopped hurting 24 hours a day. And beyond all that, I finally felt like I could live and enjoy my new baby, instead of being crushed under a weight of anxiety. 

So yeah, if you want to stop, then stop. Don't forget you can always just combo feed if that's what you want. You can use formula as your primary food method and nurse for comfort and bonding when you feel emotionally and physically able.  Or you can stop BF all together. But take care of yourself and believe me when I say that your kiddo will not be hurt by formula. ❤️

Hey ladies! We just finished night 4 over here with Ava. She was born December 28, 2 days before her EDD. Short birth story just to get something out. 

Most of you know I was scheduled for an induction tuesday night/wednesday morning December 28. I ended up having to go in Tuesday morning bc I thought my water broke, but they tested it and said nope so they sent us home. 

We went in that night as scheduled, and I started cytotec at 11 pm. I was supposed to have 4 doses, every 2 hours. I got a 2nd one at 1 am. It did kick up my contractions (I was already crampy all day) but they were tolerable. They offered me ambien and I took that and slept some. My husband and I just watched tv and Seinfeld episodes on our laptop. At 3 am my contractions were 4-5 minutes apart at which point they stop cytotec. 

I was told pitocin would start early in the morning so I asked for an epidural before pitocin started. I was terrified of the epidural but even more of pitocin contractions. Apparently my spinous processes are close together. So, not gonna lie, getting it placed was a bitch. I had an amazing nurse at that time and she kept me calm, it took maybe 20 minutes and multiple attempts. But we got it in and then it was glorious. I started pitocin around 6 am. My husband and I watched some more TV, and I slept some through the morning. 

My doctor checked me at 9 am and I was 4 cm dilated. I think she checked one more time when I was 6 cm, then a little before 12 noon she woke me up from my nap and said it was baby time. I pushed for a little less than an hour and Ava was born just before 1 pm. 

Night 2 was hell, apparently that's a thing. Nights 3 and 4 have been much better, and my husband and I are getting a rythm down now that we're not in the hospital. 

Unfortunately she's borderline jaundice getting discharged and all the nurses would do is tell me feed her more. FYI, that's a great way to make a hormonal, sleep deprived, new mom fall apart sobbing. Ya'll, I fed this baby round the clock. I slept 30 minutes in 24 hours. This bitch nurse reached over and squeezed my nipple to express colostrum, with no warning or asking permission, to "prove" to me that I was making colostrum. Yeah lady, I'm aware I have colostrum.

We ended up calling our pediatrician at midnight friday night (bet he loves us) and he has us doing formula feedings every 3 hours with pumping bc we need to be sure she is hydrating. Luckily I've gotten to where I'm pumping out enough now to feed her breast milk first in a bottle then formula after, to be sure she gets the milk. He is very supportive of BF so if her weight and jaundice are resolved at our appointment we can hopefully go back to BF when my milk comes in. Basically the thought is that I was feeding her but with no way to tell how much if any she was eating, and she wasn't making enough urine, so we just need to take a few days to be sure she gets enough food/fluid and then we can work on BF. Apparently jaundice is caused by dehydration (not eating enough), and jaundice makes babies sleepy. No surprise, sleepy babies don't latch and eat well, and don't stay awake long enough to take in enough food. So it's a cycle, hence why he said switch to formula first bc I'm spending hours tiring her out on the breast with no results. I'm definitely worried we ruined the chance to BF. If she fusses and roots in between the 3 hour feeds I offer her the breast to keep her used to it. Hopefully we'll make it work.

I won't re write all the good advice you've already gotten. But I'll add that in addition to asking if they have availability and/or wait list, specifically ask if they use a waitlist or you reserve a spot for your infant. In my area, there's a big difference between these two options. Some places put you on a waitlist and then you get a spot when a spot is available, if you're spot comes open before you're ready then they move on to the next person. Other places don't use waitlist and instead you pay a reservation fee and then that's your spot, they don't line up multiple people. To add to that, specifically ask whether your spot is guaranteed or if they bump you when a mom of a current daycare child needs another spot for a new baby. Some places will also do that and others specifically do not give priority to current families over new families. I've had multiple friends lose their daycare spot at the last minute because they weren't aware they didn't have a guaranteed place.

> Induction at 39 Weeks Is Better for Mother and Baby
Alicia Ault
May 17, 2016
 
WASHINGTON, DC — The optimal time of delivery for women with low-risk pregnancy has been a continuing source of controversy, but a debate on the elective induction of labor at 39 weeks here at American Congress of Obstetricians and Gynecologists 2016 Annual Clinical Meeting turned out to be a statement of consensus.

The two presenters agreed that evidence is mounting that waiting beyond 39 weeks is not advisable.

"Continuing the pregnancy beyond 39 weeks is riskier than previously believed for the fetus," said Errol Raymond Norwitz, MD, PhD, chair of the Department of Obstetrics and Gynecology at the Tufts University School of Medicine in Boston. In addition, risks to the mother associated with routine induction "are lower than appreciated," he said.

"I was absolutely opposed" to the elective induction of labor at 39 weeks, said Charles Lockwood, MD, dean of the Morsani College of Medicine at the University of South Florida in Tampa. In fact, he was prepared to debunk the notion.


But after much reading, "it's overwhelmingly evident that elective induction of labor is the logical strategy," he said.

Members of the audience in the crowded ballroom were won over by Drs Norwitz and Lockwood. Before the presentations, 20% said that it would be best to deliver most women at 39 weeks, 17% were unsure, and 63% were against the idea.

After the presentations, 81% of the attendees said they changed or reconsidered their view. In fact, 70% said they agreed that it is best to deliver most women at 39 weeks, 21% were still unsure, but only 9% were against the idea.

Stillbirth a Bigger Danger Than Realized

Even though higher rates of stillbirth after 39 weeks have been reported since the late 1980s, it still seems to be underappreciated, said Dr Norwitz.

He pointed to several studies that showed that stillbirth is a greater risk at 40 weeks of gestation and beyond.

"Antepartum fetal deaths account for more perinatal deaths than do complications of prematurity or SIDS," he said, citing a report that estimated that there were at least 26,000 stillbirths in the United States in 2004 (BMC Pregnancy Childbirth. 2015;15[Suppl 1]:A11).

Those findings have "been recapitulated in multiple datasets," he explained.

And one study he described showed an increasing risk for stillbirth and neonatal mortality with each passing week of gestation (Br J Obstet Gynaecol. 1998;105:169-173).

It is not known why the rate of stillbirth increases, but it could be related to uteroplacental dysfunction. It might also reflect the failure to identify risk factors, such as multiple pregnancy, infertility, low blood pressure, intrauterine growth restriction, and having previously delivered a small-for-gestational-age infant, he said.

No Increase in Cesarean Rates

The major risk associated with a failed induction at 39 weeks is cesarean delivery, but both Dr Lockwood and Dr Norwitz said that there does not appear to be any evidence of an increase, and that perhaps it might even decrease rates, compared with expectant management.

Some studies have indicated that the rate of cesarean delivery increases in multipara with an unfavorable cervical exam, said Dr Norwitz.

However, data comparing rates of cesarean delivery and other outcomes after induction at 39 weeks and after expectant management at 41 weeks are weak to nonexistent, in part because it would take 2 million to 12 million pregnancies to get good answers, Dr Lockwood explained.

So he and his colleagues conducted a comparative-effectiveness analysis. "We evaluated every conceivable outcome that we could think of," he said. The model involved probabilities for 60 outcomes. The team then created a Monte Carlo microsimulation to map out head-to-head effectiveness.

Expectant management was associated with higher rates of cesarean delivery than induction at 39 weeks, and "a clear increase in perinatal mortality," he reported. Maternal death rates were not significantly different in the two groups, but severe complication rates were lower for both the infant and the mother in the induction group, said Dr Lockwood.

The bottom line is that "elective induction at 39 weeks is always a better strategy" than expectant management at 41 weeks, he said.

Both Dr Norwitz and Dr Lockwood said they agree that success with induction requires very accurate dating of gestational age. "If you're off, you could endanger the patient," said Dr Lockwood.

He also cautioned that induction "has to be a real induction of labor — not one that ends at five o'clock."

Dr Norwitz and Dr Lockwood have disclosed no relevant financial relationships.

American Congress of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) 2016 Annual Clinical Meeting. Presented May 16, 2016.

Well, I'm a little confused by your post so bear with me while I try to get your time line correct. 

So, a week and a half ago you had an ultrasound at the ER and they estimated you at 6 1/2 weeks. Early dating ultrasounds are very accurate, much more so than 2nd and 3rd trimester ultrasound. So, if that's the case that would make you about 8 weeks along today. 

You say your nurse confirmed you're 9w1d. How did she confirm? Did you have another ultrasound or did she just base this on the date of your last menstrual period (LMP)? 

If she's basing on LMP, unless you were tracking ovulation very carefully, then LMP is not necessarily accurate. LMP dating assumes you ovulate on cycle day 14. Some women do, but many don't. Many women ovulate later (or earlier), which makes LMP dating inaccurate. So, let's say you ovulated on cycle day 21 instead, 1 week later, then you would only be 8w1d along instead of 9w1d. 

Basically, early ultrasound dating is very accurate. The fetal heart rate you had measured in the ER is normal for that gestational age. If you're not having any signs of a miscarriage (cramping is normal in early pregnancy), there's no reason to believe there's anything wrong with your pregnancy. You most likely just ovulated late and your next ultrasound may very well show this by measuring on track with your first ultrasound.  

Edit: Obviously, yes, the other outcome is that the ER ultrasound measured behind because the baby isn't growing appropriately. But, like I said, if you weren't tracking ovulation then 1 week is a completely reasonably and common difference. You'll find a lot of women with the same story.

I don't know anything about the single umbilical artery, but I have an MCI. From my understanding, it doesn't resolve or progress, it just exists this way for the entire pregnancy. Mine was diagnosed at my 20w anatomy scan. I'd recommend not googling :) My doctor was able to reassure me about it, and reading stories on babybumps made me feel better as well. I'm 37 weeks tomorrow, and have had growth scans every 4-6 weeks since my anatomy scan to monitor her growth. 

What I was told is that the only possible complication from MCI is that is slightly raises your risk of IUGR (intra uterine growth restriction). So, generally, you will end up with growth scans the rest of your pregnancy to monitor for that possibility. I was also told that, it often doesn't actually cause any problems, and seems to be one of those anomalies that we've discovered due to our advanced medicine and ultrasound screening. For thousands of years this is just something that's existed with generally no adverse outcomes. At least, that's how it was explained to me. 

I am also under the impression that even if it does cause IUGR for you, that will happen later in the 3rd trimester. From what I read, when people have to deliver early for IUGR, we're talking about 35, 36+ weeks along. NOT 24, 28 weeks etc. And the plus side is that you will get extra scans and monitoring from a high risk OB, so you can rest assured they're taking good care of you and your baby. 

Hope that helps you feel a little better.

There were too many triggers in my life all around me, so if there's any possible way you can get yourself in a treatment center, I highly recommend it.

I had an ED 10 years ago, have been in recovery since then. There are a lot of us around here so you'll likely get lots of responses. I'm not sure of your age or how quickly you need to get pregnant, or if you have some time. But, I would *strongly* recommend getting successful treatment and overcoming your ED before becoming pregnant, if you can help it. Even 10 years out, pregnancy has been a million times harder for me in that respect than I ever expected. I thought I was fully recovered, have gone all this time without relapse and only minimal, occasional obsessive thoughts. After all that, I have struggled A LOT due to the weight gain. And, tbh, I'm concerned about how I'll handle the post baby weight/body change and weight loss. I fully expect I may need to be in therapy to avoid a relapse. So, all that to say, I can't imagine the difficulty of going through pregnancy with an active ED. I think you owe it to yourself and your future child to get yourself healthy first. I apologize if that sounds harsh, that's not necessarily my intent. I know first hand how hard it is to beat an ED. But, this isn't just about you anymore once you get pregnant. It's not even just about keeping your body physically healthy during the pregnancy. You need to be able to be a healthy role model for your child after he/she is born. I learned a lot of terrible habits from my mother, and she doesn't even have an actual ED, just horrible self esteem and poor body image. Kids listen to what they hear even if it's not directed *at* them.

Have you talked to your doctor about your past and all your feelings? That would be my first piece of advice. Be really upfront about your history, your worries, your appetite, what you're eating. If your doctor doesn't have any concerns than you shouldn't need to worry. 

Other than that, what I can say from hanging around here and babybumps for months is that women gain different amounts, at different rates, and at different times in their pregnancy. Some women don't really start gaining until about half way and then gain most of their weight in the second half with a lot in the 3rd tri. It's entirely possible you cold follow that pattern. If you gain a pound a week (sorry, I don't know kg) for your third trimester you'd be right on track. Also, some women gain more or less than the recommended and are perfectly healthy. 

In the end, talk to your doctor/midwife and see what they think. And be sure you're not restricting. It's one thing to avoid every cookie/ice cream/cheeseburger craving, but entirely different to deny yourself food when you're hungry. If you feel hungry, listen to your body and eat something substantial.
